title: Humaid-Ner: A Disaster Tweet Dataset for Joint Named Entity Recognition and Event Classification Via Uncertainty-Weighted Multitask Learning
venue: The Asian Bulletin of Big Data Management
problem_statement: Disaster-related social media benchmarks provide document-level category annotations but lack span-level entity labels (such as location, casualties, displaced counts, or requested supplies) required for operational humanitarian response coordination. Additionally, joint multi-task training of dense token-level named entity recognition and single sentence-level event classification leads to severe gradient asymmetry and task conflict (2,688 NER token signals vs. 1 classification signal per example), causing classification macro-F1 to progressively degrade under fixed-weight multi-task learning.
domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media NLP (Twitter/X Disaster Tweets in English), Multitask Learning, Named Entity Recognition
theoretical_framework: Homoscedastic uncertainty-based multi-task loss weighting (Kendall et al., 2018) derived from a probabilistic log-likelihood formulation with learnable task variance parameters, coupled with the hierarchical representation learning hypothesis (Liu et al., 2019 / MT-DNN) positing that lower transformer layers capture universal linguistic representations while upper layers encode task-specific patterns.
methodology: Constructed the HUMAID-NER dataset by extending 60,000 English tweets from the HumAID benchmark across 19 disaster events into 10 operationally motivated entity types (yielding 21 BIO classes) via a three-stage hybrid auto-labelling pipeline combining a spaCy transformer backbone (en_core_web_trf), domain-specific EntityRuler patterns, and regular expressions with priority- and length-based overlap resolution. Designed a joint multitask architecture using a shared RoBERTa-large encoder (24 layers, 355M parameters) with a linear token projection head for sequence labeling and a dual-pooled classification head concatenating the [CLS] embedding and mean non-padding token representations (2,048 dimensions). Trained the model using homoscedastic uncertainty loss weighting with learnable task log-variance parameters (s_NER, s_CLS) and a two-stage training schedule: Stage 1 (epochs 1–7) jointly trains all 24 encoder layers; Stage 2 (epochs 8–15) freezes the bottom 18 layers (reducing active parameters from 355M to 47M) to specialize upper layers and task heads. Developed and deployed a real-time web dashboard for simultaneous single-forward-pass inference.
datasets: HUMAID-NER (60,000 English tweets from 19 natural disaster events between 2016 and 2019 sampled from HumAID, annotated with ~175,000 entity spans across 10 disaster-specific types in BIO format; partitioned into 72% train [43,200 tweets], 14% validation [8,400 tweets], and 14% test [8,400 tweets] stratified by 10 humanitarian categories)
HumAID benchmark (77,637 English tweets from 19 natural disaster events labelled across 10 humanitarian categories)

metrics: Entity-level span micro-F1 via seqeval (exact entity type and span boundary match required)
Macro-averaged F1 across 10 humanitarian categories for event classification
Balanced validation combined score: Score_val = 0.5 * F1_NER + 0.5 * F1_CLS
Classification-first deployment policy (prioritizing classification macro-F1 with combined score breaking ties)

key_findings: Introduced HUMAID-NER, the first disaster-domain named entity recognition dataset extending HumAID with 60,000 tweets and ~175,000 entity spans across 10 operational entity types (LOCATION, CASUALTY, DISPLACED, REQUEST, RESOURCE, RESCUE, DISASTER_TYPE, ORGANIZATION, PERSON, NUMBER) mapped to 21 BIO classes.

Empirically identified task conflict and gradient asymmetry under fixed-weight joint training, where dense token-level NER supervision (up to 2,688 signals/sample) dominated sentence-level classification (1 signal/sample), causing classification macro-F1 to peak at epoch 3 (0.748) and degrade by 1.4 points to 0.734 by epoch 15 despite monotonic reduction in training loss.

Demonstrated that Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting dynamically balances task losses via learnable log-variance parameters, preventing classification degradation and stabilizing multitask training dynamics.

Found that two-stage layer-freezing training (freezing layers 1–18 in Stage 2) produced the largest classification gain (+1.6 macro-F1 points, reaching 0.761) by reducing active parameters from 355M to 47M and enabling task-head and upper-layer specialization without eroding shared representations.

The proposed joint RoBERTa-large framework achieved 0.841 NER span micro-F1 and 0.761 classification macro-F1 concurrently on the validation split, matching or exceeding single-task RoBERTa-large baselines (0.730–0.750) without incurring classification performance penalties while delivering full entity extraction capabilities.

Demonstrated operational viability via a real-time web dashboard capable of extracting typed entity spans and predicting humanitarian event categories simultaneously in a single forward pass without task-specific inference latency overhead.
scope_and_delimitations: Text corpus restricted to English-language disaster tweets sampled from 19 natural disaster events between 2016 and 2019 in the HumAID benchmark.
Dataset size delimited to a balanced 60,000-tweet subset across 10 humanitarian categories rather than the complete 77,637 HumAID corpus.
Entity taxonomy delimited to 10 operationally motivated humanitarian entity types (21 BIO classes) excluding generic newswire categories.
Empirical evaluation delimited to the held-out validation split (8,400 tweets) to intentionally reserve the test set against overfitting.
Hardware constraints on TPU v3-8 restricted experimental ablations to single-run point estimates without multi-seed variance analysis.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Limitations include no human inter-annotator validation of the auto-labelled annotations, English-only coverage (2016–2019), validation-split-only reporting (testset evaluation reserved to prevent overfitting), and single-run point estimates for all ablation results (multi-seed variance analysis was precluded by TPU compute budget and is left for future work).
limitations.summary: The dataset relies on an automated three-stage hybrid labelling pipeline without human inter-annotator agreement verification; the corpus is restricted to English tweets from 2016–2019 across a 60,000-tweet subset; evaluation reports only validation split results with test set evaluation reserved; ablations are single-run point estimates lacking multi-seed variance analysis due to TPU compute limits; and direct empirical gradient conflict diagnostics were not collected.

generalizability_gap: The dataset and joint framework are limited to English-language tweets from 19 natural disaster events (2016–2019), leaving unexamined non-English and multilingual disaster communications, low-resource regional dialects, multimodal crisis streams (paired text and imagery), and non-natural disaster domains such as industrial accidents, armed conflicts, or public health emergencies.
methodological_gap: The auto-labelling pipeline lacks formal human inter-annotator agreement metrics (such as Cohen's or Fleiss' Kappa) to quantify pseudo-label noise; direct gradient diagnostics (such as gradient cosine similarity or conflicting gradient norm tracking across shared layers) were not measured to provide direct mechanistic proof of gradient interference; and the ablation study lacks multi-seed statistical variance bounds.
future_work: Combine PCGrad gradient surgery with Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting to eliminate destructive gradient interference without excessive computational overhead.
Scale the three-stage auto-annotation pipeline to annotate the remaining tweets in the full 77,637-tweet HumAID corpus and new disaster events.
Extend the joint multitask architecture to multilingual crisis tweet analysis using XLM-RoBERTa paired with soft gazetteers.
Conduct direct empirical gradient tracking across encoder layers during multitask training to evaluate gradient conflict dynamics.
Perform multi-seed variance analysis across all model configurations to establish statistical significance bounds.
